offence_severity: imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than seven years but which may extend to imprisonment for life
physical_harm: deceased consumed poison, leading to her death
number_of_offences: charged under Section 304-B, upheld under Section 304-B
key_evidence_accepted: Consistent and confidence inspiring testimony of deceased’s father (PW4) about continuing harassment meted out to deceased on account of dowry, and the prosecution having satisfied the necessary ingredients u/s.304B IPC
witness_credibility: Both the Trial Court and the High Court found the evidence of P.W.4 to be reliable and consistent despite thorough cross-examination. The testimony of PW4 is found to be consistent and inspiring confidence by this Court as well.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 2008; Trial judgment: 15.03.2010; High Court decision: 15.03.2010; Supreme Court decision: 28.05.2021
legal_representation: Counsel for the accused: Rishi Malhotra; Counsel for the State: Ms. Jaspreet Gogia, Karanvir Gogia, Ms. Shivangi Singhal
appeal_history: Trial court: Convicted; High Court: Upheld conviction; Supreme Court: Dismissed appeal
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the death of the deceased occurred within seven years of marriage under suspicious circumstances, and there was a proximate and live link between the dowry demand and the death. The accused forged medical records to show a cordial relationship, and the deceased had informed her father about harassment due to dowry demands.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the Courts below applied the presumption under Section 113-B of the Evidence Act without satisfying the basic ingredients of Section 304-B, IPC. They claimed the deceased was happy with the appellant, there was no cruelty, and a conviction under Section 304-B could not be sustained without charges under Section 498A.
legal_principle_applied: The Court applied the principle that the prosecution must establish the necessary ingredients of Section 304-B, IPC, and once satisfied, a presumption of causation under Section 113-B, Evidence Act arises, which the accused must rebut.
precedent_relied_upon: Satbir Singh v. State of Haryana 2021 AIR 2627; Kamesh Panjiyar v. State of Bihar [2005] 1 SCR 903; Kans Raj v. State of Punjab, [2000] 3 SCR 662; Rajinder Singh v. State of Punjab, [2015] 2 SCR 835
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the prosecution satisfied the necessary ingredients of Section 304-B, IPC, and the accused failed to rebut the presumption of causation under Section 113-B, Evidence Act.
